G8A01: Direct FSK shifts the oscillator itself between two frequencies under control of the digital data line. Keying a CW input or sending audio tones into an SSB transmitter makes AFSK or tones, not direct FSK.
G8A02: Phase modulation conveys information by shifting the phase angle of the RF carrier. Phase inversion is just a 180 degree flip, not the name of the modulation process.
G8A03: Frequency modulation varies the carrier's instantaneous frequency in step with the information. Frequency conversion only moves a signal to another frequency, as a mixer does, without carrying information.
G8A04: A reactance modulator changes the reactance seen by an amplifier stage, which shifts the phase of the RF passing through it, so the result is phase modulation. Used on an oscillator instead, the same circuit gives FM.
G8A05: Amplitude modulation varies the RF amplitude, and so its instantaneous power, with the modulating signal. FM and phase modulation keep the amplitude constant.
G8A06: All listed items are true of QPSK31: its four phase states make it sideband sensitive, its convolutional encoding gives error correction, and it fits in roughly the same 31 Hz bandwidth as BPSK31.
G8A07: Single sideband sends only one sideband with no carrier, so it needs about 2.4 to 3 kHz, the least of these phone emissions. FM and phase modulation phone use far more, about 10 to 16 kHz.
G8A08: Overmodulation distorts the signal and generates splatter, spreading energy far outside the normal channel, so the main effect is excessive bandwidth that can interfere with nearby stations.
G8A09: FT8 sends its symbols as 8-tone frequency shift keying, using eight tones spaced 6.25 Hz apart for a total bandwidth of about 50 Hz.
G8A10: Flat-topping is distortion when too much drive or microphone gain pushes the amplifier past its peak output, clipping the top of the envelope. That clipping makes splatter and a wider signal.
G8A11: The modulation envelope is the outline formed by joining the peaks of the modulated RF wave; in AM it follows the shape of the audio. It is not the carrier or the bandwidth.
G8A12: QPSK uses four carrier phases, 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees, each standing for a pair of bits, so it carries two bits per symbol.
G8A13: A link budget adds transmit power and antenna gains, then subtracts losses such as feed line and path loss, to get the signal level seen at the receiver. The sum of gains minus losses alone leaves out transmit power.
G8A14: Link margin is how far the received power is above the minimum level the receiver needs. For example, a -90 dBm signal into a receiver that needs -110 dBm gives a 20 dB margin.
G8B01: In a superhet the local oscillator is tuned so that it mixes with each desired RF signal to land on the fixed IF. The RF input is the incoming signal, not the input you tune.
G8B02: Image response is reception of a signal on the other side of the local oscillator, 2 x IF away from the wanted signal, which also mixes down to the IF. Front-end filtering and a high IF reduce it.
G8B03: Heterodyning is mixing two RF signals in a nonlinear device to produce sum and difference frequencies. Synthesizing means generating a frequency, not combining two signals.
G8B04: A frequency multiplier makes a harmonic of a lower-frequency oscillator, for example a 12.21 MHz stage multiplied by 12 to reach 146.52 MHz. A mixer would add or subtract two frequencies instead.
G8B05: Odd-order products such as 2F1 - F2 and 2F2 - F1 fall close to the original frequencies, often inside the passband, which makes them the troublesome ones. Even-order products land far away and are easy to filter.
G8B06: By Carson's rule, bandwidth = 2 x (deviation + highest modulating frequency) = 2 x (5 kHz + 3 kHz) = 16 kHz. Adding 5 and 3 to get 8 kHz forgets the factor of two for both sidebands.
G8B07: The multiplication factor is 146.52 / 12.21 = 12, so the oscillator needs only 5,000 Hz / 12 = 416.7 Hz of deviation to produce 5 kHz at the output frequency.
G8B08: Modes such as FM, RTTY and many digital modes transmit at full power almost continuously, so their average power is close to peak and can exceed the transmitter's average power rating. You may need to reduce power for them.
G8B09: A receive bandwidth matched to the signal lets in all of the signal but as little noise as possible, giving the best signal-to-noise ratio. FCC rules do not set receiver bandwidths.
G8B10: Sending more symbols per second needs a wider bandwidth; the occupied bandwidth rises roughly in proportion to the symbol rate. Lower symbol rates allow narrower signals, which is why weak-signal modes are slow.
G8B11: A mixer's output contains the sum and difference of the LO and RF frequencies, for example 14.2 MHz and 9 MHz give 23.2 MHz and 5.2 MHz. Filters then pick the one used as the IF.
G8B12: Intermodulation is the unwanted mixing of two or more signals in a nonlinear circuit, producing spurious outputs at combinations of their frequencies. Heterodyning is the same mixing done on purpose.
G8B13: The order of a product is the sum of the multipliers, so 2F1 - F2 is 2 + 1 = 3, an odd-order product. 5F1 - 3F2 is 8th order and 3F1 - F2 is 4th order, both even, so not every listed product is odd-order.
G8C02: WSPR (Weak Signal Propagation Reporter) stations send low-power beacon transmissions that are decoded and reported online, showing where a band is open. PSK31 is a keyboard chat mode, not a beacon system.
G8C03: The header of a packet frame carries the routing and handling information, such as the source and destination callsigns and digipeater path. The data payload follows it.
G8C04: Baudot (ITA2) is a 5-bit code used for RTTY, with start and stop bits added to each character. The 7-bit code with parity is ASCII.
G8C05: NAK means negative acknowledgment: the packet arrived with errors, so the receiving station asks for it to be sent again. An ACK would mean it was received without error.
G8C06: When too many retries fail, an ARQ link gives up and the connection is dropped. The protocol does not change character sets or reroute packets because of it.
G8C07: FT8 can decode signals down to about -20 dB signal-to-noise ratio in a 2.5 kHz bandwidth, well below what a human ear can copy. MSK144 is for short meteor scatter bursts, not continuous weak signals.
G8C08: PSK31 uses Varicode, which gives common lower case letters short codes and upper case letters longer ones, so typing in capitals slows the transmission. PSK31 has no error correction and needs less power than RTTY.
G8C09: A mesh network routes data through whichever nodes are available, so if one node fails, a packet can still reach its destination through another path. More nodes do not raise signal strength.
G8C10: FEC sends redundant information along with the data, so the receiver can rebuild missing or damaged bits without asking for a repeat. A single parity bit can only detect some errors, not fix them.
G8C11: The two FSK frequencies are called mark and space, terms carried over from telegraph and teletype practice. Dot and dash describe Morse code.
G8C12: PSK31 sends characters in Varicode, a variable-length code in which common characters have the shortest bit patterns. Viterbi is a decoding method, not the character code.
G8C13: Vertical lines on either side of a data or RTTY trace on a waterfall show spurious sidebands from overmodulation, often from too much audio drive. Lower the audio level until they disappear.
G8C14: On a waterfall, frequency runs across the screen horizontally, signal strength is shown by brightness or color, and time scrolls down the screen vertically.
G8C15: FT8 reports are signal-to-noise ratio in dB referenced to a 2.5 kHz bandwidth, so +3 means the signal is 3 dB above the noise in that bandwidth. It is not an S-meter reading.
G8C16: DMR, D-STAR and System Fusion are digital voice modes. FT8, FT4 and FST4 are weak-signal data modes, and Winlink and PACTOR carry text and email.
G9A01: The characteristic impedance of a parallel conductor line depends on its geometry: the spacing between the conductor centers and the conductor radius. It does not depend on line length or frequency.
G9A02: High SWR means more power travels back and forth on the line, so more is lost to heat in a lossy line. On a low-loss line the extra loss from moderate SWR can be small.
G9A03: Window line, the ladder-style twin lead with slots in the insulation, has a nominal characteristic impedance of about 450 ohms. 50 and 75 ohms are typical coax impedances.
G9A04: Power is reflected at the feed point when the antenna's feed point impedance differs from the feed line's characteristic impedance. Running an antenna at resonance does not by itself cause reflections.
G9A05: Coax loss increases as frequency goes up, mainly because of skin effect in the conductors and dielectric loss. That is why a run of RG-58 that is fine on 80 m can be very lossy at UHF.
G9A06: Feed line loss is usually listed in decibels per 100 feet at a stated frequency. Ohms describe impedance, not loss.
G9A07: Standing waves disappear only when the load impedance equals the line's characteristic impedance. Choosing a special line length does not stop reflections; it only changes what impedance is seen at the far end.
G9A08: A matching network at the transmitter only changes what the transmitter sees; the mismatch at the antenna still sets the SWR on the line, so it stays 5:1. The line SWR could only drop if the match were made at the antenna.
G9A09: For a resistive load, SWR is the larger impedance over the smaller: 200 / 50 = 4, so 4:1. SWR is written with the larger number first, so 1:4 is not used.
G9A10: For a resistive load, SWR is the larger impedance over the smaller: 50 / 10 = 5, so 5:1. SWR is always written with the larger number first.
G9A11: Line loss weakens the reflected wave on its way back, so SWR measured at the transmitter end reads lower than at the antenna. A very lossy line can hide a bad antenna match.
G9B01: A random wire fed directly from the transmitter uses the station as part of the antenna system, so the rig and other equipment may carry significant RF current. That can cause RF burns and interference in the shack.
G9B02: Sloping the radials of an elevated quarter-wave ground plane downward raises the feed point impedance from about 36 ohms toward 50 ohms, giving a better match to coax.
G9B03: A quarter-wave ground-plane vertical radiates equally in all compass directions, so it is omnidirectional in azimuth. It is not isotropic because it puts little energy straight up.
G9B04: A dipole in free space radiates most broadside to the wire and almost nothing off its ends, giving a figure-eight pattern at right angles to the antenna. The nulls are off the ends.
G9B05: Below about 1/2 wavelength, ground reflections push most of the dipole's radiation upward, so at high elevation angles its azimuthal pattern is almost omnidirectional. This is the basis of NVIS operation.
G9B06: Radials for a ground-mounted vertical are laid on the ground surface or buried a few inches deep, spreading out from the base. Raising them high makes it an elevated ground plane instead.
G9B07: As a horizontal dipole is lowered toward the ground, coupling to the ground lowers its feed point impedance steadily below the free-space value of about 72 ohms. At 1/10 wavelength it is well under 50 ohms.
G9B08: Toward the ends of a half-wave dipole the current falls and the voltage rises, so the feed point impedance increases steadily from about 72 ohms at the center to a few thousand ohms at the ends.
G9B09: A horizontal HF antenna does not rely on the ground as part of the antenna, so it avoids the ground losses that weaken a vertical's efficiency. Verticals need a good radial system to cut those losses.
G9B10: Using length in feet = 468 / frequency in MHz, 468 / 14.250 = 32.8 feet, about 33 feet. The 16 foot option is roughly a quarter wave.
G9B11: Using length in feet = 468 / frequency in MHz, 468 / 3.550 = 131.8 feet, about 132 feet. 263 feet would be a full wavelength.
G9B12: Using length in feet = 234 / frequency in MHz for a quarter wave, 234 / 28.5 = 8.2 feet, about 8 feet. 16 feet would be roughly a half wave.
G9C01: Larger-diameter elements have a lower Q, which widens a Yagi's usable bandwidth. Loading coils do the opposite and narrow it.
G9C02: The driven element of a Yagi is roughly a half-wave dipole, about 1/2 wavelength long. The parasitic elements are cut a little longer or shorter than that.
G9C03: In a three-element Yagi the reflector is a little longer than the driven element and the director a little shorter. That arrangement makes the beam fire toward the director.
G9C04: dBi compares gain to an isotropic radiator and dBd to a dipole, which already has 2.15 dBi of gain, so gain in dBi is 2.15 dB higher. A 7 dBd beam is about 9.15 dBi.
G9C05: A longer boom with more directors concentrates more energy in the forward direction, so gain increases and the beam gets narrower, not wider.
G9C07: Front-to-back ratio compares the power radiated in the main lobe with the power radiated in the opposite direction, usually given in dB. A higher ratio means better rejection off the back.
G9C08: The main lobe is the direction in which a directive antenna radiates its strongest field. It is not about current or voltage points along an element.
G9C09: Stacking two identical Yagis 1/2 wavelength apart and feeding them in phase doubles the effective aperture, so gain rises about 3 dB, which is a doubling of power. 6 dB would need four times the power.
G9C10: All listed items are adjustable design choices: boom length, number of elements and element spacing all trade off forward gain, front-to-back ratio and SWR bandwidth on a Yagi.
G9C11: A beta or hairpin match is a short, shorted transmission line stub across the feed point that acts as an inductance to match a Yagi's low feed impedance to the feed line.
G9C12: A gamma match taps the driven element at a point of zero RF voltage at its center, so the element can be mounted directly to the boom without insulation. It does use a series capacitor and works on one band.
G9D01: A horizontal dipole only 1/10 to 1/4 wavelength high sends most energy nearly straight up, which the ionosphere reflects back down nearby, ideal for 40 m NVIS by day. Verticals put little energy at high angles.
G9D02: An end-fed half-wave antenna is fed at a voltage maximum where current is low, so its feed point impedance is very high, typically a few thousand ohms. A matching transformer is used.
G9D03: A halo is a horizontal loop-like dipole bent into a circle, so it radiates fairly evenly in all directions in the plane of the halo, giving horizontally polarized omnidirectional coverage.
G9D04: Traps are parallel tuned circuits that act as switches, cutting off part of the antenna on higher bands so one antenna can work on several bands. They are not filters for spurious signals.
G9D05: Stacking horizontal Yagis vertically narrows the main lobe in elevation, putting more energy at low angles and adding gain. Azimuth beamwidth is set by each Yagi and stays about the same.
G9D06: A log-periodic antenna works over a wide frequency range, often covering several bands with good SWR. It gives less gain per element than a Yagi.
G9D07: In a log-periodic antenna the element lengths and spacings change by a constant ratio along the boom, a logarithmic progression that makes its properties repeat with frequency.
G9D08: A screwdriver antenna uses a motor to move a contact along its base loading coil, changing the inductance to tune the antenna and adjust the feed point impedance for each band.
G9D09: A Beverage is a long, low wire used for directional receiving on MF and low HF bands, where it hears weak signals well despite being too inefficient for transmitting.
G9D10: A small loop's nulls are broadside to the loop, perpendicular to its plane; its maximum response is in the plane of the loop. Direction finders turn the loop to find the sharp null.
G9D11: A multiband antenna is designed to work on several frequencies, so it often also radiates harmonics that fall on those bands, giving poor harmonic rejection.
G9D12: An inverted V is a dipole hung from one central support with its two legs sloping down toward the ground. An inverted L is fed at one end and is not a center-fed dipole.
G0A01: RF energy is non-ionizing, so its known effect on the body is heating of tissue, much like a microwave oven. It cannot cause radiation poisoning.
G0A02: All listed items are true: duty cycle sets average power, frequency sets which exposure limit applies, and power density is the quantity measured against the limits.
G0A03: All listed methods are accepted: calculations based on OET Bulletin 65, computer modeling, or measurement with calibrated equipment can show your station meets the exposure limits. [97.13(c)(1)]
G0A04: Time averaging means the total RF exposure is averaged over a set period, 6 minutes for controlled and 30 minutes for uncontrolled exposure, so short transmissions count for less.
G0A05: If an evaluation shows the fields could exceed the limits, the licensee must act to keep people out of those fields, for example by reducing power or restricting access. [97.13(c)(2), 1.1307(b)] Neighbors cannot waive the limits.
G0A06: A station that does not qualify for an exemption must do an RF exposure evaluation, and OET Bulletin 65 gives the accepted methods. [97.13(c)(2), 1.1307(1)(b)(3)(i)] No FCC permission or special filter is involved.
G0A07: Exposure is averaged over time, so a mode with a lower duty cycle, such as SSB or CW, delivers less average power and permits higher transmitted power than a mode keyed constantly. No duty cycle is exempt.
G0A08: Licensees must evaluate RF exposure and keep people out of any areas found to exceed the limits. [97.13(c)(2)] Posting the rule or notifying neighbors is not required.
G0A09: Accurate RF field strength measurement needs a calibrated field strength meter with a calibrated antenna or probe. An SWR meter measures conditions on the feed line, not the field.
G0A10: If the main lobe could overexpose a neighbor, make sure the antenna cannot be pointed at them when they are present, for example with rotation limits. A higher gain antenna would make it worse.
G0A11: An indoor antenna sits close to people, so make sure the MPE limits are not exceeded in occupied rooms. Putting it near your operating position increases your own exposure.
G0A12: FCC RF exposure rules cover every station, amateur included, whose time-averaged power is over 1 milliwatt; at 1 milliwatt or less a source is exempt regardless of distance. [1.1307(1)(b)(3)(i)(A)] Amateurs are not exempt, and there is no 500 watt threshold.
G0B01: Fuses or breakers go only in the hot wires, which carry the voltage. Fusing the neutral or ground could open them and leave equipment live and unsafe.
G0B02: The National Electrical Code calls for at least AWG 12 copper on a 20 ampere circuit. Smaller wire such as AWG 14 is rated for only 15 amperes and could overheat.
G0B03: AWG 14 copper wiring is rated for 15 amperes, so use a 15 ampere fuse or breaker. A larger breaker would let the wire overheat before tripping.
G0B04: The lightning protection ground should be outside the building, where the feed lines enter, so a strike's current goes to earth before it gets inside to the station equipment.
G0B05: A GFCI trips when current leaks from a hot wire directly to ground, since the hot and neutral currents no longer balance. Normal current from hot to neutral does not trip it.
G0B06: The National Electrical Code covers electrical safety, including the wiring and grounding of an amateur station. Bandwidth, modulation and RF exposure are set by FCC rules instead.
G0B07: Check that the harness is rated for the climber's weight and is within its service life before climbing. Holding on with one hand leaves only one hand to work, and heavy tools are better hauled up separately.
G0B08: Before climbing a tower with powered devices, lock out and tag all circuits that feed it so no one can switch them on while you are up there. The tower should stay grounded.
G0B09: Generators give off deadly carbon monoxide, so run them only in a well-ventilated area, never indoors. Fuel should be stored away from the hot generator, and the frame should be grounded.
G0B10: Lead from solder can get on your hands and then into food, so wash your hands after soldering. RF energy cannot turn lead into a poisonous gas.
G0B11: All ground rods and other grounds must be bonded together so there is no voltage difference between them during a strike. Ground wires should run straight, without sharp bends.
G0B12: An interlock removes dangerous voltages when the cabinet is opened, protecting anyone who reaches inside. It is a safety switch, not a temperature or overvoltage cutout.
G0B13: Lightning arrestors go where the feed lines enter the building, so surge current is sent to the outside ground before reaching the station.
